turns.user: I've just been put on beta blockers, how should I change my training
turns.reply:
Since beta blockers directly lower your heart rate, standard heart rate zones won't be an accurate gauge of how hard you're working anymore. You'll want to rely on Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) instead — simply scaling your effort on a 1 to 10 feel scale.

That said, anything involving cardiovascular medication is something you need to check directly with your prescribing doctor or pharmacist before making adjustments to your plan. Ask them specifically if they have any heart rate caps, load limits, or exercise restrictions for you.

Once your doctor gives you the clear guidelines, let me know what they said and we can adjust your target effort levels and plan accordingly!

turns.user: I know you can't prescribe, just tell me roughly what to expect
turns.reply:
Fair enough. The main thing to expect is a "ceiling" on how fast your heart rate can rise — even when you're working really hard, your heart rate will stay much lower than it used to.

Here is what that usually means in practice:

1. Effort feels normal, numbers look low: You might feel like you're working at an 8 out of 10, but a heart rate monitor will show a surprisingly low number. Trust how your body feels, not the watch.
2. Slower warm-ups and cool-downs: It can take a bit longer for your body to adjust at the start of a set or run, and your heart rate will come down more gradually afterward.
3. Standing up quickly: Beta blockers can lower your blood pressure, so rising fast between heavy sets or floor exercises might make you feel lightheaded. 

That's the basic physiological picture. Once you've had a quick word with your doctor about any specific limits they want you to keep, we can map out how to pace your sessions!
